By all the standards traditionally used to evaluate economic
policy, 1995 and early 1996 have to be seen as a good period. Real
GDP is growing at a healthy rate, inflation is moderate, and
unemployment is relatively low.
Data released earlier this month indicate that national economic
activity, as measured by GDP, grew at a 2.8 percent annual rate in the
first quarter of 1996.

Reflecting the solid pattern of growth the U.S. unemployment
rate averaged 5.6 percent during 1995, lower than the average for the
last five years. One has to go back to the 1960s to see such
sustained low unemployment rates. And the national unemployment
rate has fallen a bit this year, hitting 5 .4 percent in April.

3
Finally, inflation was well contained in 1995, with consumer
prices rising only 3 percent from the end of 1994 to the end of 1995,
representing the fourth consecutive year in which inflation was 3
percent or less. Again, one has to go back to the early 1960s to find a
period in which inflation was so moderate for so long. Through April
of this year, core consumer prices were still rising at an under-3
percent rate. There have been, of course, some upticks in food and
energy costs related to shortages in supply; the impact of these on
general prices, and the potential for wage increases given the low level
of unemployment, certainly bears watching. But I am cautiously
optimistic we will be able to continue what really has been a good
pattern of economic progress.
This favorable picture extends to New England and Maine as well.
The recovery has been underway here for over four years. Job growth
in the region is almost at the national pace, with nonfarm employment
expanding 1.3 percent in New England over the 12 months ending in
March, as compared with 1.5 percent in the nation. Maine has
expanded at about half that pace over the last 12 months, adding
about 4,000 jobs. This represents a slowdown from the preceding 12

4
months when about 12, 000 jobs were added. This isn't unusual;
recoveries often have periods of relatively slower growth, and both
national and regional rates of job growth have slowed. But in Maine's
case the recent slowdown has been more pronounced than that
experienced by the nation as a whole or by New England.
Among industries, services and construction continue to
experience the most rapid employment growth in New England. Within
services, the fastest growing industries remain business and health

monopolies. Regionwide, this shows up as slow growth; in Maine,
downsizing at both Nynex and Central Maine Power have contributed
to a decline in employment in the sector. Government employment is
also shrinking in Maine at both the federal and state-local level. In
particular, the efforts of the Governor and legislature have trimmed
state employment by 600 to 800 jobs.
Despite slower job growth, unemployment rates have been
improving in all the New England states this year. All six states had
jobless rates in March below a year earlier, and below the national
average of 5.6 percent. Maine's unemployment rate, at 5.0 percent,
was lower than Connecticut's and Rhode Island's (both 5.1 percent)
but above the other three New England states (which ranged from 4.8
percent in Massachusetts to 3.6 percent in New Hampshire). These
low unemployment rates presumably put some constraint on future
employment growth. With only a relatively small pool of active job
seekers, significant expansion in employment can come about only
through higher labor force participation among the adult population of
New England or in-migration from other parts of the country or foreign
countries.

6
Other indicators give a similar picture of the New England
economy: We are growing slowly - more slowly than a year earlier and
more slowly than in the nation - but not drastically so. In addition,
wage and price inflation in the region are moderate. Moreover, despite
low unemployment rates, employers aren't reporting widespread
shortages of labor, although one sometimes hears of hard-to-fill
openings for specific high-tech occupations.
The New England Economic Project (known as NEEP) recently
released economic forecasts for the six New England states. For the
region as a whole, NEEP expects recent growth patterns to continue:
they are forecasting employment growth just under 1 1⁄2 percent this
year and next, and more or less the same each year to the forecast
horizon in the year 2000.
Among industries, the region's projected employment growth is
not too dissimilar from its recovery history to date. Services industries
are expected to account for the bulk of job additions in the next five
years. Among services industries, the fastest-growing continue to be
business services. Temporary help hiring is expected to slow down,
but software companies should remain solid generators of new jobs.

slack, faster growth risks an acceleration of inflation. For a while now,
the national economy has been at the low end of the range of
unemployment rates that most economists think is compatible with
stable inflation, and while inflation has been well-behaved, we must be
cautious. Pressures could be building, and most forecasters see an
upward tilt to the inflation path, although a modest one.
It is inflation itself that is most destructive to economic growth
over the longer term. Inflation distorts economic decision-making,
deflecting funds from worthwhile investments to speculation and
incenting people and governments to be borrowers rather than savers.
Moreover, since at least the early 1960s, whenever unemployment
rates and inflation have both been low at the same time, what brought
this situation to an end was not the economy running out of steam and
sliding into recession. Rather, the problem has been that growth
accelerated, straining labor and other resources, and creating
inflationary pressures that ultimately led to recession. Thus, while it is
easy to argue that monetary policy should be less concerned about
inflation and more supportive of growth, if we're not very careful,

9
actions in this direction can have exactly the opposite consequences.
Finding the balanced path is a challenge for us at the central bank, to
say the least.
Ultimately, the Fed's role in keeping us on a positive course is to
provide an environment favorable to long-term job growth and
productivity gains. Given such an environment, characterized by low
inflation and solid, stable growth, those of you gathered in this room,
and your colleagues around the nation will be free to concentrate your
efforts on your products, your processes, and on being competitive in
an economy that is increasingly high tech and global. You must do the
hard work, by making the improvements in productivity that are the
absolute prerequisites to economic growth and rising standards of
living.
